2.text: teams are stronger, though the mountainous roads of that country are more trying

3.text: for the dogs than the level tundra. Chukchee teams are not as strong and well

4.text: trained, nor are the drivers so skilful, as are the Koryak or the Kamchadal.

5.text: Maydell asserts that on the Lower Kolyma a team of from twelve to fourteen

6.text: dogs can haul a load of 60 puds (2160 pounds Avoirdupois), which would

7.text: average about 154-180 pounds for each dog.¹ This is evidently a mistake, since

8.text: even postal reindeer-teams often carry only 6 puds on each sledge, which makes

9.text: 3 puds (108 pounds Avoirdupois) for each reindeer. The dog-drivers of the

10.text: Kolyma allow for each dog (according to a local saying) “1 pud to carry, 1000

11.text: herrings to store” (i. e., for winter food). The “herrings” mentioned are, properly

12.text: speaking, not herrings at all, but of the species Coregonus albula.

13.text: Middendorff says that on the Yenisei each dog is reckoned as able to

14.text: carry not more than 100 Russian pounds’ weight (90 pounds Avoirdupois).

15.text: This is also too high an estimate, and seems improbable, since a few lines

16.text: before he calls the system of attaching the dogs on the Yenisei undeveloped

18.text: In dragging a heavily loaded sledge, the dogs take advantage of its

19.text: impetus, for they can draw it along only at a rapid pace. When stopped,

20.text: they cannot even start again without the help of the driver. When going up

21.text: hill, the driver has to walk along and pull the sledge with his utmost strength,

22.text: and at especially steep places he sometimes has to partially unload. Every

23.text: five or six miles the dogs are given a rest of about five or ten minutes, after

24.text: which they start again with renewed vigor. In the middle of the day there

25.text: will be given a longer rest (Plate VI, Fig. 4), perhaps three-quarters of an

26.text: hour, while the driver melts snow for drinking, and cooks food for himself.

27.text: While in harness, the dogs are perhaps still wilder than when at large.

28.text: A wild reindeer, a hare, or the fresh smell of seal, is quite enough to lure them

29.text: off the track, regardless of the driver. When passing by a reindeer-herd, the

30.text: dog-driver may always calculate that the excited animals will carry him into the

31.text: middle of the herd, and may even succeed in seizing a reindeer, notwithstanding

32.text: the exertions of the driver to arrest the heavy sledge with the brake.

33.text: The dogs preserve their hunting qualities, even while in harness. A

34.text: Chukchee driver, meeting a white fox on the tundra, will set free his fleetest

35.text: dog in the hope of good luck. However, hunters say that the speed and

36.text: acuteness of the dog for hunting are spoiled by the harness, since its back

37.text: grows stiff. The Kamchadal hunters, when tracking a bear in late spring,

38.text: sometimes let the team overtake the bear, and, while the struggle is going

39.text: on, wait their chance for a sure shot. The bear has no advantage in this

40.text: struggle, and often is so entangled with straps and traces as to become quite

41.text: helpless. The keen-scented dog, able to find the seal-hole for the hunter,

42.text: may also be found among the team-dogs.
